Welcome, everybody. Let me tell you a secret about small talk in Canada. It's not about information. Nobody really needs to know that it's cold today. We know it's cold. It's about connection. The two safest topics are the weather and hockey. If you don't like hockey, that's fine, but don't say it too loudly in Toronto. And here's the most important rule: when someone asks you a question, answer it, and then ask one back. How about you? Do you? Have you? That's all it takes. Oh, and you'll hear the word sorry all the time. We say it even when it's not our fault. Don't worry. So do the British.

Today on the show, a few phrases that sound like agreement but often aren't. Take I see your point. Lovely phrase. But very often what comes next is the word but. I see your point, but I think you're wrong. So it really means: I understand you, and I don't agree. Then there's fair enough. That one is more honest. It means: I accept what you said, even if it wasn't my first choice. You want to leave at nine? Fair enough. And my favorite: that makes sense. Sometimes it means I agree. Sometimes it just means I understood. My advice? Listen to the tone of voice, not just the words. The tone tells you the truth.

When I moved abroad, the first month was hard. Not because I didn't understand people. I understood most things. The problem was reacting. Someone would tell me a story and I'd just stand there, smiling, saying nothing. People thought I wasn't interested. What changed everything was simple. I started reacting with short answers. Really? So did I. Neither have I. Oh, have you? It sounds silly, but it works. One day my neighbor said, I've never caught a fish in my life. And I said, neither have I, but I'd love to try. Now we go fishing every Sunday. We get along really well. We just needed someone to break the ice.
